processing: Not a single recipe: the name covers both green and black tea. The green is made in the usual way for Chinese greens, fixed, shaped and dried into straight, neat leaf.
harvest_season: Varies by producer; as with other Sichuan greens, spring tea is the one prized.
appearance_dry: The green style is straight and neat, tender green and even.
appearance_liquor: Little is documented for the green style; expect a clear, bright green cup, as is typical of its class.
appearance_wet: Little is documented; expect tender green buds and leaves in the green style.
taste_profile: The green style is described as mellow and brisk with a sweet return and a lasting chestnut aroma.

brewing.notes: For the green style only. The black tea sold under the name needs its own treatment, so check the class first.

vintage_note: The name alone does not tell you the class or the age. The green tea is sold as the current harvest, as usual for Sichuan greens; the black follows its own norms, so read the producer and harvest date on the pack.
description:
Tianfu Longya is less one tea than a Sichuan name used across a wide area, and it is sold as both a green and a black tea.

Growing areas are described in broad terms: the hills around the rim of the Sichuan basin and the basin's own low hills. That breadth matters, because two packs may share little beyond the name.

The green style is described as neat, straight tender leaf with a mellow brisk taste and a chestnut aroma. The black style is reported as fine, tight, gold-tipped leaf with a citrus-candy scent.

When buying, treat the producer as the real information. Check the class, the county and the harvest date on the pack.
history: Little is documented about this name as a tea rather than as a brand. It is listed among the province's well-known teas today.
